Backups & restore

A backup is a copy of the panel's database: users, nodes, settings, the audit log and the secrets in it.

Treat a backup bundle as secret material

The database holds node API keys and the Telegram bot token as written — there is no at-rest encryption, by design, because encrypting them would only move the key to another file on the same host. What protects them is the filesystem: the data and backup directories are 0700, and the database and every .ovmbak bundle are 0600. Move any off-site copy over an encrypted channel.

Take a backup now

Bundles land in /var/lib/ovmanager/backups, and the newest 14 are kept unless you change that. Reaching for the panel's web UI is not required at any point — which matters, because the usual moment you want a backup is the moment the panel is unhappy.

A bundle is a gzipped tar with a .ovmbak suffix, holding a consistent SQLite snapshot of the database, a manifest, and a checksum file. It is verified as it is written and again as it is read, so a truncated or edited bundle is refused rather than restored over your live data.

A daily backup

This is a systemd timer, so it keeps running even if the panel is stopped. The panel has its own scheduler too, under Settings → Backup — off by default, with its own time and retention. Using both is redundant; pick the one that matches how you operate, and remember that only the timer survives a stopped panel.

Off-site copies

A daily backup on the same disk is not a backup. The scheduled backup can push the newest bundle to another machine: fill in a target like backup@server:/backups/panel and, after each automatic backup, the newest file is copied there with rsync (or scp when rsync is not installed).

  • The transfer uses plain SSH with key-based login and BatchMode — no password prompts, ever.
  • The target machine must already accept your key, and the target folder must already exist.
  • Success or failure is written to the Audit Log. Nothing else on the remote side is created, rotated or cleaned up — retention is yours to manage there.

Restoring

From the CLI

ovm restore with no name lists what is available and changes nothing. Naming a bundle restores it, with the service stopped and restarted around the swap.

From the panel

Settings → Backup accepts an uploaded bundle and restores it atomically:

  • Writes are refused — HTTP 503 — until the swap has finished, so nothing is half-written against a database being replaced.
  • The database being replaced is kept as a fallback.
  • The restored database is migrated on the spot, so an older bundle comes back at the current schema version rather than needing a manual step.

What is in a backup, and what is not

ItemBacked up by ovm backup
Users, expiry, quotas, tagsYes — in the database
Nodes and their API keysYes — in the database
Settings, admin accounts, audit logYes — in the database
Panel TLS key and certificateNo — they live outside the database
VPN users, certificates and configsNo — those live on each node, under /var/lib/ovnode and /etc/openvpn

So a complete disaster-recovery plan has two halves: the panel database here, and each node's own state. Back both up, and remember that node data is only rename-safe if you keep the same --name.
